content.thinking:
I'm planning the phoenix design in one careful pass without testing — Genshin-style, wings spread, perched on a small ember rock base so its feet touch the ground, with rough proportions around 1.2m body height.

Working out the skeleton: hips root, spine chain running through tail/hips/chest, then a neck chain branching up to the head, defining joint positions so the body curves naturally from tail to head.

For the head I'm placing the head and jaw joints at the top of the neck chain, aiming forward and slightly down, using explicit bone references for clarity. For the tail, I'm setting up a chain of long flowing feather streamers fanning backward and down toward the ground, giving it a flame-like tail silhouette.

Now I'm designing a feather helper that extrudes a leaf-shaped outline along a direction vector with a sharp tip, then coloring each feather with a gradient that shifts from crimson at the base through orange to gold at the tip, wrapped in a cel-shaded paint style.

Now I'm working out the rachis highlight band, then laying out the wing skeleton: shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand-tip joints positioned to give a spread, slightly raised wing pose with roughly 3.2 total span, defining the joint chain names and coordinates for each segment.

Working out primary feather placement and angles...

For the extrude orientation, I need to be careful with the up vector since it must be perpendicular to the direction vector—I'll compute it by projecting out the component along x and normalizing, rather than assuming a default up works.

Actually, feathers should lie flat in the wing plane, so I need the outline width to go along the horizontal perpendicular to feather direction, with thickness being vertical, meaning I should use up cross x for the wide axis instead. I'll tilt primaries slightly upward for a dramatic upswept look, and assign feathers to appropriate bones (wrist for primaries, elbow for secondaries, shoulder for inner feathers), then layer smaller coverts above the main feathers in rows with slight vertical offsets.

Now I'm adding glowing flame-shaped cards at feather tips, tail, and crown using SVG flame textures with gradients for an elemental fire motif, and planning to loft the body shape along a spine-and-neck path.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up station points with widths and heights from tail to neck to define the body's loft profile, and establishing a root "hips" joint with a spine chain branching from it toward the neck.

I should exclude the tail chain from the body loft and give it its own feather sweep separately, with the tail bones parented to the hips. Then I'm sketching leg placement for a perched bird pose, setting hip joints and foot IK targets.

For legs, I'm working out a three-segment limb (thigh, tibia, tarsus) reaching from hip to foot, with bend directions alternating forward then back at the knee and hock so the stance looks natural, keeping the final segment vertical into the toes.

Now I'm defining the leg chain names and mirroring both sides by flipping the hip x-offset, assigning "L" or "R" suffixes, and setting up the thigh as a tapered sweep with an orange feather puff at the hip. For the toes, I'm planning each foot to have three forward digits and one back digit, built as small two-joint chains extending from the foot point.

Working out toe geometry and claw placement...

For the plinth I'm lathing a rock shape with a wider base tapering up, giving it dark stone coloring with glowing orange cracks, then attaching it rigidly to the root bone.

Setting the toe target height just above the plinth surface, scattering a few small glowing ember cubes on top for detail. For the head, I'm shaping an anime-style bird head using a scaled ellipsoid with a swept cone-shaped beak positioned at the front.

Shaping the upper beak with a curved bezier sweep for a hooked tip, and adding a smaller lower jaw beak attached at a joint bone so it can open and close. Now I'm setting up the glowing anime-style eye decals.

For the crest I'm adding a plume of five feathers sweeping backward and up, using my feather helper with gold-red gradients anchored to the head bone, plus small glowing flame cards at the crest tips. I'm also considering small extruded cheek feathers pointing backward for extra ruffle detail.

Now I'm scattering body feather cards across the chest with a teardrop scallop texture gradient from red to gold, tinted white, sized small and leaning back with gentle bend so the silhouette stays fine-grained. For body coloring I'm layering a countershade gradient from crimson back to gold belly, applying cel shading on top, and adding a fur-edge effect along the breast for texture.

I'm defining the fur-edge zigzag pattern with teeth and period parameters along the body's z-axis, wrapping it in cel shading so shadows derive correctly from the resolved paint, and settling on a crimson-to-gold-to-pale-gold palette for the overall bird.

Now I'm thinking through ornamentation: gold filigree jewelry like anklets, a crown circlet with a glowing ruby, shoulder bands, and hanging tassels, plus a gold gorget collar swept around the neck using a loop surface along the neck joints.

Adding a ruby pendant gem at the collar front, figuring out placement via ray-casting toward the neck center to position it correctly.

I also want glowing wrist gems with gold torus rings, plus gold wing-arm bracers at the elbow using a loop sweep along the arm frame.

Writing flame SVG gradient...

For the flame cards, I'm collecting frames at the feather tips and orienting them to flow backward with a cross-pattern so they're visible from every angle around the tail.

I'm also considering adding fiery wisps along the wing's leading edge, using frames lifted slightly above the arm sweep to create a glowing outline. Tallying up the part budget across wings, tail, and crest, I'm estimating around 250 parts plus sweeps, well within limits, with glow cards batched into single meshes per texture.

Checking triangle counts, the feather extrusions should run roughly 50 tris each, keeping total geometry around 8k triangles, which is manageable. For the tail, I'm planning 7 curved streamer feathers fanning back and down from the base, making sure the ends stay above floor level even with the plinth's radius, and using bezier sweep ribbons instead of straight leaf shapes for a more elegant look.

For the tail ribbons themselves, I'm using flat elliptical cross-sections (wide in x, thin in the normal direction) swept along bezier paths so each feather lies horizontally like a real fanned tail feather, with 9 total sweeps starting near the tail base and spreading outward.

Working out the taper function so each feather narrows smoothly to a point near the tip rather than cutting off abruptly, using a power-of-sine curve for the width profile.

For coloring, I'm defining a gradient ramp across each feather from deep maroon through red and orange to a gold tip, mixing palette colors with a helper function, and reusing the mix utility already exported from the paint module. I'm also wrapping the lit color in a cel-shading quantizer that checks the light dot product against a threshold and falls back to a shadow tone, resolving the paint at a point/normal pair using the ambient sample context set by the outer call.

Now I'm working out texture resolution: feathers cover roughly 12 square meters total, so with a 2048 paint atlas I get about 2mm texel density, which is fine for the subtle chevron barb striping and gold rachis stripe I want to add along each feather's spine.

For the color ramp, I'm defining a crimson-to-gold gradient across the feather length, going from deep maroon at the root through red and orange to a pale gold-white tip, mimicking a Genshin-style primary feather look. Covert rows higher on the wing get a shifted version of this same ramp, biased toward gold and orange rather than starting at the dark root color.

I'm also sorting out the joint hierarchy for the wing: shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints carry the arm, with primary feathers attached to the wrist joint, and I'm considering adding dedicated fan-spread joints so the feathers can splay out realistically.

Now I'm defining the feather outline geometry as an asymmetric leaf shape with eight points tracing from a rounded root to a sharp tip and back, adding a slight jagged notch near the tip for a flame-like silhouette, with constant extrusion thickness since a y-based taper wouldn't work properly here.

For wing tilt, I'm computing the width vector as the cross product of up and the feather's direction, which gives consistent orientation on both wings even though the cross product sign flips between left and right sides. I'm staggering neighboring feathers vertically to create a layered overlap effect, then checking the overall wing planform—shoulder to wrist to primary tips—and realizing the resulting wingspan comes out to roughly 4.6 meters, appropriately massive for a mythical phoenix body around 1.3 meters tall.

I'm scaling things down slightly: shortening the arm reach and primary length so the half-span comes to about 2 meters, giving a 4-meter total wingspan paired with a roughly 1.6-meter tall body, which feels more balanced for a large phoenix. Now I'm defining the joint positions along the arm—shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand tip—with mirrored x-coordinates for left/right symmetry, then working out the direction vectors for each primary feather based on an outward sweep angle and a vertical lift that's steeper for outer primaries and flatter for inner secondaries and tertials, and computing the segment lengths along the arm chain to space the primaries correctly.

Working out the lengths, angles, and widths for secondaries and tertials...

Now I'm defining a function that interpolates wing angle along the arm, then using it to place two rows of covert feathers with decreasing length and slightly offset positions near the leading edge.

Still working out feather distribution...

That covers the covert feathers near the body in crimson. Now I want to add gold tassels dangling from the wrist bracers and tail base, like decorative cord fringe hanging downward, placed at the bottom of each wing's wrist point.

I'm also planning a gold circlet on the head, done as a torus ring positioned at the forehead and tilted forward slightly to sit like a brow band.

Checking the horizontal torus orientation at y≈1.405 — that lines up with the 35° elevation point on the gem sphere, so a ring rotated flat should sit right at that surface height.

I'm sizing the eye decals now, placing them symmetrically at ±40° azimuth, 5° elevation, with dimensions around 0.05 by 0.068.

Now I'm laying out the body as a loft through a series of width/height stations running from the lower torso up through the hips, chest, and neck to the head sphere, making sure the hips aren't too narrow. I still need to work out the bone chain linking spine, neck, and hips for the skeleton.

I'm figuring out the shoulder joint parented to the spine, then sweeping the arm as a tapered chain with an evenly spaced radius profile. For the legs, I'm placing the hip joints inside the belly volume and calculating target foot positions with segment lengths summing to roughly the vertical drop needed.

Now I'm working out the toe geometry — three forward toes splayed at angles around the z-axis plus a back toe, each built as a tapered tube chain parented to the foot joint with decreasing radii toward the tip.

For claws, I'm angling a spike off the last toe segment that dips down and sinks slightly into the plinth surface, keeping it shallow since the plinth isn't the floor itself. Then I'm adding gold-toned scale paint texture to the tarsus and leg surfaces.

Now I'm adding a gold anklet band as a torus around the leg joint, orienting it using the bone's direction so it wraps naturally around the hock.

Next I'm working out the tail ribbons: nine fanned strands radiating from the tail root, with angles spread roughly between -50 and 50 degrees, making the central ribbons longer and curving each one's endpoint outward and backward for a flowing arc shape.

I'll anchor the ribbon start to the tail chain's root joint, then plan nine ribbons with varying lengths (symmetric around the center, from shorter at the edges to longer in the middle), plus a few extra-long thin streamers for variety.

I'm spacing the ribbons by angle offsets and adding slight vertical layering so overlapping ribbons near the root don't visually collide, with each one kept thin. I'll also add a couple of extra-long curled plumes near the center for a dramatic tail accent.

I'm positioning the flame tail tips so they stay above the floor, then working out a set of crest feathers sweeping from the head backward, with curved bezier paths that vary slightly in length and offset to create a layered look.

Now I'm adding small flame cards at the crest tips, tail tip, and wing primary tips—tiny upright wisps that stand at each point, double-sided so they're visible from any angle, plus extra flame wisps running along the top edge of the arm.

Then I'm scattering a ring of ember cards around the plinth edge, and covering the body with hundreds of textured feather cards whose base grey-white texture gets tinted by the body's paint color, varying lean and bend slightly for a natural scattered look.

I'm also adding smaller cheek and head-back feather cards filtered to the skull surface, plus a gold collar sweep ring at the neck joint to mark the transition between head and body.

For the collar, I'm placing it at the upper neck joint with a small loop radius and lifting it slightly, adding a row of inline gold beads around it plus a front-facing gem pendant using a ray hit test to anchor an octahedron glow shape in red-orange.

Now I'm adding the skull decal for eyes and a crimson-to-gold face color split using a fur-edge cel shader based on vertical position, with the boundary set below the midline so the lower face reads gold. For the iris color, I'm leaning toward a teal/cyan accent to contrast against the crimson head, giving it a stylish Pyro-with-cool-accent look.

Now I'm working through smaller features: setting the beak to a warm cel-shaded yellow tone, placing jaw and head joints with specific position and aim offsets for the rig, and deciding to skip nostril and ridge details to keep things simple while keeping the ruby gem accents red and the eyes as the sole teal highlight.

I'm also sketching out where the skull sphere and eye azimuths sit, then thinking through how to add small decorative gold elements like elbow/wrist bracer rings or a wrist gem onto the arm sweep without overcomplicating the geometry.

Writing the imports and setup code...

Still refining the ramp function...

Writing paint function logic...

Now I'm drafting the feather function signature, importing the Joint type from the skeleton module for the bone parameter.

Still writing feather logic...

Still writing wing chain logic...

With spacing settled, I collect wisp frames along the arm for flame placement, then set up the glow effect using flame-shaped cards with randomized variation and directional flow. Now I'm sketching the tassel texture with a gold knob, cord, and fringe details rendered as SVG paths.

For the hanging cards I decide on placement at wrist and elbow cuffs, collar pendant, and other attachment points, orienting each frame upward with a 180-degree lean so they drape naturally downward. Finally I move to the plinth, defining a lathed rock profile as a closed loop of points and adjusting the foot height to rest properly on top of it.

I'm detailing the rock material with glowing orange crack patches set against dark volcanic tones, then attaching the plinth rigidly to the hip joint and scattering small emissive icosahedron embers along its rim for a fiery glow, with flame-themed cards arranged in a ring around the base.

Moving to the skeleton, I'm setting up the hip joint as the spine root, then building a spine chain with catmull curves through spine1, spine2, and chest, followed by a neck chain into a head joint and jaw, and finally a tail chain of three joints curving backward from the hips, with the body loft and ribbons set to follow along it.

I need to make sure the tail stays clear of the plinth geometry so it doesn't intersect, and I'm building the main body surface as a loft across stations bound to the spine, neck, and hips bones. One subtlety I need to handle is that when multiple bones share the same starting point on the spine (like hips and spine1), the span assignment should favor whichever bone is listed last so the skinning weights resolve correctly.

I realize if hips is listed after spine1 in the bone array, spine1 ends up unused for skinning since hips takes over that span -- so I should reorder to list hips first, which lets spine1 actually contribute. I'm also thinking through the coloring: adding a gold "bib" patch on the chest using a normal-based axis so the front-facing area reads warm while the rest stays crimson, picking an axis direction that captures the forward-facing chest region correctly.

Checking that the body loft section defaults to an appropriate shape and that the skull geometry parameters are set reasonably.

Now I'm scattering cheek and back-of-head cards using a surface filter that excludes the front face, then placing eye decals via angular positioning on the skull surface with mirroring for symmetry, guarding against null hits.

Next I'm adding a gold circlet with a torus geometry, positioning and rotating it around the head, accounting for the head's elliptical scale so the circlet sits correctly at an angled height above center.

Setting up the beak with curved bezier tubes for upper and lower sections, tapering the radius from base to tip and positioning them against the skull surface with appropriate widths.

Now I'm defining the leg geometry, computing hip and foot points and building limb chains using those positions.

Working out the toe geometry next — placing toe chains at angles spreading from the foot tip, sweeping tube segments for each digit, and adding claw spikes pointing forward and down from the toe ends. Checking that toe radius embeds properly into the plinth without poking through.

Now I'm adding leg scale texturing, gold ankle/hock rings positioned along the leg segment using torus geometry with a horizontal axis, and tallying up the total joint count across hips, spine, neck, tail, wings, legs, and toes to roughly 42. Moving on to wing arm bone radii and tapering.

For paint efficiency, I'm reusing the body paint for arm shading since positions are independent, and reconsidering the feather paint count — with roughly 148 distinct paints needed, I'm caching them by rounding feather length to 0.05 buckets so similar lengths share a cached Paint object, keeping the cache local to the build function so repeated builds stay deterministic.

Writing ribbon function...

I'm shaping the ribbon so its radius starts thin, swells toward the middle, and tapers again — giving it a leaf-like profile — with a rigid bone attachment and a flat six-sided cross-section for thinness, then coloring it with a gradient ramp that shifts from a dark maroon base to a bright tip color based on position along the curve.

Now I'm deciding against adding a rachis stripe pattern to the ribbons since the flat geometry makes it unreliable, opting for a simple color ramp instead, and starting to define an array of tail ribbon lengths spread symmetrically at angles up to 44 degrees to form a fan shape.

Writing ribbon placement code...

Checking that the fan of nine ribbons overlaps correctly near the root while spreading apart toward the tips, then moving on to set up the crest ribbons using a similar symmetric index range.

Now I'm working out tip-frame collection for flame wisps at the tail ends, verifying that Vector3 inputs work fine for frame generation. I'm scattering feather cards across the body using filtered hit points, checking that the color tint and lighting behave correctly with the greyscale texture, then moving on to set up the neck collar loop with a lift parameter.

I'm sweeping the collar path into a tube, adding a beaded ring around the neck using sphere parts positioned along a second offset loop, and setting up a ray-cast pendant on the chest that embeds a ruby octahedron with a glow effect.

Now I'm working out the arm details: wrist and elbow ruby accents placed via sweep frames, gold cuff rings looped at the arm joints, and hanging tassel cards attached below the cuffs. I'm calculating the exact frame positions by accounting for arm radius so the tassels sit flush against the bottom of each cuff rather than floating or clipping through the mesh.

I'm also checking overall bounds — confirming the plinth sits flat at y=0 with nothing sinking below, and that the crest, flames, and wing primaries stay within a reasonable height ceiling around y≈1.8. Then I'm writing SVG textures for the flame and feather details: the flame uses layered gradient paths for a glowing orange-to-white core, while the feather texture has a vertical white-to-grey gradient with a midrib line for a subtle plume effect.

Now I'm shifting into the TypeScript build function, importing types like Joint, Paint, Chain, and Frame, setting up color constants, and defining typed arrays for frames and outlines to keep everything strict and type-safe. Writing builder code...

I'm defining a leaf-shaped outline function and a wing feather placement closure that computes the feather's base position, direction vector, bone attachment, and length/width, calling into a feather-generation function for each placement along the arm chain.

I'm now looping through tertiary, secondary, and primary feather positions to build covert rows with slight length/width/angle variations, and tagging some feathers near the wingtip with flame-effect markers. I'm also roughing out counts (around 148 extruded feather parts total) and planning a secondary set of small flame wisps distributed along the arm, while deciding to skip the shoulder epaulette detail.

Writing the piecewise interpolation helper...

I'm also setting up the angle, vertical offset, and length tables that drive the wing's shape, confirming the shoulder-to-tip bend looks right, and finishing up the head crest and eye before composing the final output.
